stem: In a frequency distribution, the class mid-points are plotted on the X-axis and the corresponding frequencies on the Y-axis, and consecutive points are joined by straight line segments. The diagram so formed is called a:

per_option_rationale.rationale: A histogram uses class boundaries (not mid-points) on the X-axis and draws adjacent rectangles whose areas represent frequencies; it is not formed by joining plotted points.
A frequency polygon is constructed by plotting the mid-point of each class against its frequency and connecting successive points with straight lines; it directly matches the description.
An ogive (cumulative frequency curve) plots cumulative frequencies against class boundaries, not individual frequencies against mid-points.
A bar chart uses discrete categories on one axis and draws separate rectangular bars; it is not applicable to a continuous frequency distribution described by mid-points and joined lines.

explanation: The frequency polygon is the graphical form that uses class mid-points on the X-axis, plots frequencies, and joins consecutive points with line segments - exactly the description given.

explanation_sections.punchline: The decisive identifier is 'mid-points joined by line segments' - that is precisely the frequency polygon, not the histogram (which uses bars between class boundaries).
explanation_sections.approach: State the property: a frequency polygon joins (mid-point, frequency) pairs with straight lines. Contrast the confusables: histogram draws rectangles between class limits; ogive plots cumulative frequencies; bar chart applies to discrete data with gaps between bars.
explanation_sections.lesson: Whenever a graphical description mentions class mid-points joined by lines, it is always a frequency polygon.
explanation_sections.timing: 20 seconds by direct recall. The only trap is confusing histogram (rectangles, class limits) with frequency polygon (points joined, mid-points).
